status: UNPUBLISHED partial editorial/art draft; not registered in app
sourceReview: Read all bundled BSB Psalm 22, Psalm 13, Psalm 42, Matthew 27, Mark 15 and Hebrews 2 before writing. Gospel uses are identified as later narrative connections; the heading does not identify a historical occasion.

verses.title: Why have You forsaken me?
verses.heading: The lament addresses God from within an experience of abandonment
verses.meaning: The repeated my God keeps the cry directed toward God even as the speaker asks why rescue seems far away. These are words of anguish, not a detached explanation of why suffering happens or a statement that the sufferer has lost all faith. The heading names David and a tune but supplies no particular incident from his life. Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 later place this opening cry on Jesus’ lips. That Christian connection matters deeply, while the psalm should also be heard as a whole lament that moves through distress toward an answer and shared praise. Its later turn does not silence the opening question.
verses.contextTitle: A heading, a cry, and a later Gospel connection
verses.context: The bundled BSB includes the entire musical heading within verse 1, including The Doe of the Dawn. It gives no melody or scene involving a doe to reconstruct. Read the opening beside verses 21–24, where an answer and attention to the afflicted become explicit.
explore: My God, my God
The speaker still addresses God personally. The question gives a voice to felt abandonment without supplying a simple cause for it.
Far from saving me
Distance expresses the experience of rescue delayed. The symbolic ravine illustrates that feeling without claiming to locate God.
Jesus’ later use
Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 echo this opening in their accounts of Jesus’ death. This later connection should be explained without inventing the psalm’s original circumstances.
verses.reflect: When help feels distant, what question would you most want to put into words? Who could listen to it without rushing you toward an answer?
verses.alt: A solitary anonymous adult stands on a limestone ridge above a mist-filled ravine before dawn.

verses.title: Day and night
verses.heading: The cry continues without an experienced answer or rest
verses.meaning: The speaker describes calling by day and by night, with no answer and no rest. Time itself seems filled by the plea. The verse does not name a cause of sleeplessness or diagnose a condition; it gives language to prolonged distress. Continuing to address my God holds relationship and the experience of silence together. The poem does not blame the speaker for failing to pray enough. Readers do not need to turn a restless night into a test of spiritual worth, and receiving practical care is compatible with the honest prayer voiced here.
verses.contextTitle: Persistence before the turn to remembered trust
verses.context: Verse 2 expands the distance described in verse 1 into day and night. The Yet of verse 3 then turns toward God’s holiness. Psalm 42:3 also brings tears and day-and-night distress together, in its own separate lament.
explore: I cry out
This describes repeated appeal, not prayer withheld. The lack of an experienced answer is part of the complaint the poem permits.
I have no rest
The speaker names the burden of the night. The empty room and lamp are symbolic artistic additions, not objects described in the verse.
verses.reflect: What has felt exhausting to carry for a long time? What kind of support or rest would you welcome alongside your own words of prayer?
verses.alt: A small clay lamp burns in an empty stone room as a fading moon and first daylight appear through the window.

verses.title: Yet You are holy
verses.heading: The speaker remembers God’s holiness amid unanswered cries
verses.meaning: Yet marks a turn, but it does not announce that the distress has ended. The speaker addresses God as holy and enthroned on Israel’s praises while still living with the unanswered cry of verses 1–2. The throne language expresses divine rule in the setting of communal worship; it does not describe a human-shaped body sitting in the sky. The memory of praise stands beside pain rather than cancelling it. Readers can recognize that tension without being told that singing correctly will force rescue or that lament dishonors God.
verses.contextTitle: Communal praise remembered inside a personal lament
verses.context: Verse 3 moves from the speaker’s day-and-night cry to Israel’s praise. Verses 4–5 continue the turn by recalling the ancestors’ trust and deliverance. Later, verses 22–25 bring the speaker’s own praise into the assembly.
explore: Yet
This word turns the speaker’s attention without reporting a change of circumstances. Hope and distress remain in the same prayer.
Enthroned on the praises of Israel
The language joins holiness, rule and the community’s praise. The painting shows anonymous worshipers and leaves God unseen.
verses.reflect: What belief or memory remains significant to you when your experience feels at odds with it? Is there room to name both without resolving the tension today?
verses.alt: A small anonymous assembly stands in quiet worship in an imagined hilltop courtyard among olive trees.

verses.title: Our fathers trusted
verses.heading: The prayer reaches back to remembered deliverance
verses.meaning: The speaker recalls the trust of earlier generations and the deliverance they received. Our fathers connects the personal lament with a community’s remembered story. The verse names no individual ancestor or particular rescue, so the study does not supply one as the psalm’s proven setting. This recollection makes the current experience of silence more painful as well as providing language for hope. It must not be turned into a charge that the sufferer has less faith than those who were delivered. The poem has already shown the speaker calling persistently upon God.
verses.contextTitle: Ancestral memory that sharpens the present question
verses.context: Verse 4 follows the mention of Israel’s praise and leads into the parallel recollection in verse 5. The contrast with the speaker’s experience becomes especially clear in verse 6, which begins But I am.
explore: Our fathers
The phrase reaches toward preceding generations within the community. It does not identify a single biography to illustrate as a literal event.
They trusted and You delivered
The repeated trust recalls a received answer. The speaker’s present distress is not evidence that trust is absent or defective.
verses.reflect: What stories of help or endurance have been passed on to you? Do they bring comfort, hard questions, or a mixture of both?
verses.alt: Three anonymous older travelers follow a rocky hillside path toward a sheltered olive valley.

verses.title: They cried and were set free
verses.heading: The remembered answer contrasts with the speaker’s own cry
verses.meaning: The earlier generations cried out, were set free, and were not disappointed in their trust. This repeats the pattern of verse 4 with an emphasis on crying and its answer. The speaker has also cried out, as verse 2 makes clear, so the contrast is not between faithful ancestors and a person who refuses to pray. The tension lies between the remembered deliverance and the present experience. The line recalls those earlier answers; it does not guarantee that every faithful person will avoid prolonged suffering or imply that someone still waiting has been rejected.
verses.contextTitle: A second line of memory before But I am
verses.context: Verses 4–5 form a paired recollection of trust and deliverance. Verse 6 will then give the speaker’s painful self-description. Reading the pair with verses 1–2 keeps its remembered answers from becoming an accusation against the person lamenting.
explore: They cried out to You
The ancestors’ appeal resembles the speaker’s own cry. The parallel intensifies the question rather than explaining the distress away.
Were not disappointed
The line celebrates remembered help. It is not a verdict on people whose distress has not yet changed.
verses.reflect: When you hear someone else’s story of an answer to prayer, what does it stir in you? How could you speak honestly about your own experience?
verses.alt: Four anonymous adults emerge through an open stone gateway toward a quiet valley in gentle daylight.

verses.title: Scorned and despised
verses.heading: A painful self-image gives voice to social humiliation
verses.meaning: But I am brings the remembered trust of earlier generations into sharp contrast with the speaker’s humiliation. The worm image expresses how diminished and despised the sufferer feels under scorn; it is not a statement that any person has no human dignity. The following lines describe others mocking and taunting the speaker, giving this feeling a social setting within the poem. The study does not identify those people or invent an event from David’s life. An anonymous seated person in the painting responds to the pain without turning the poetic image into a literal worm or inviting the reader to accept contempt as truth.
verses.contextTitle: Self-description framed by remembered trust and public scorn
verses.context: The verse follows the ancestors’ deliverance and is followed by gestures of mockery in verse 7. Its severe image should be heard as the sufferer’s expression of humiliation, while verse 24 later affirms attention to the afflicted.
explore: But I am
The turn brings the lament back from communal memory to the speaker’s own painful experience. The contrast is central to the passage.
A worm and not a man
This is a dehumanizing image voiced in distress. Explaining its force does not require endorsing the speaker’s apparent worthlessness.
Scorned and despised
Others’ contempt contributes to the pain. The text does not supply their names, identities or a reason that would justify their conduct.
verses.reflect: What words of contempt have been difficult to shake off? What would it be like to describe their impact to someone who treats you with dignity?
verses.alt: An anonymous adult sits alone on a low stone outside an imagined village, head lowered and hands resting on knees.

verses.title: The mockers’ gestures
verses.heading: Public scorn leads into a quotation in the next verse
verses.meaning: The lament now describes the people who see the speaker: they mock, sneer and shake their heads. The colon matters because verse 8 continues with their taunt. These actions belong to the mockers, not to God or to the poem’s instruction for how readers should behave. Matthew 27:39 and Mark 15:29 later describe head-shaking mockery in their accounts of Jesus’ suffering. That connection should be read with care, while the psalm itself leaves its mockers unnamed. It supplies no basis for assigning a collective religious or ethnic identity to them.
verses.contextTitle: A sentence that continues across the verse boundary
verses.context: The gestures of verse 7 prepare the direct speech of verse 8. Keep the speaker’s report distinct from the mockers’ words. The later Gospel parallels belong to their own narrative contexts, rather than identifying the psalm’s original onlookers.
explore: All who see me
The expression conveys the scope of public humiliation from the speaker’s perspective. It is not a list of people whose identities can be reconstructed.
Shake their heads:
The colon leads directly into the following taunt. Reading only verse 7 would leave that sentence unfinished.
Later Gospel echoes
Matthew 27:39 and Mark 15:29 echo the gesture in accounts of Jesus’ suffering. Neither connection makes mockery a reliable judgment about the sufferer.
verses.reflect: What happens when others treat someone’s distress as a spectacle? What small response could help preserve that person’s dignity?
verses.alt: An anonymous seated adult is isolated from three distant people who turn away and gesture dismissively on a stone street.

verses.title: Trust turned into a taunt
verses.heading: The mockers challenge God to rescue the sufferer
verses.meaning: The quotation continues the mockers’ speech from verse 7. They turn the speaker’s trust in the LORD into a taunt, challenging God to rescue the person He supposedly delights in. Their words should not be presented as the narrator’s reliable explanation of how God acts. Matthew 27:43 later uses closely related language in the mockery directed at Jesus. In both reading contexts, suffering must not be treated as proof that someone is unloved by God. The full psalm later affirms that God attends to the afflicted person’s cry, but this early section first allows the wound caused by such religious ridicule to be heard.
verses.context: Verse 7 introduces the onlookers and their gestures; verse 8 supplies their direct speech. Verse 9 then turns back toward the speaker’s own appeal to God, so the quotation must not be allowed to erase the change of voice.
explore: He trusts in the LORD
The mockers refer to the sufferer in the third person. Their comment is hostile speech reported by the lament, not advice from the study.
Let the LORD deliver him
The challenge makes rescue into a public test of divine regard. The text does not ask readers to impose that test on someone in distress.
Since He delights in him
The taunt questions a relationship through visible suffering. Later verse 24 should be read alongside it without dismissing the pain of the insult.
verses.reflect: Have words about faith ever been used to dismiss your pain or someone else’s? What would a more compassionate response sound like?
verses.alt: An anonymous adult stands below a closed wooden gate while two distant people on a terrace gesture dismissively.
